spec.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
spec.conclusion: For every t>0, the density e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on R^n, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. In particular E(t)=E(s) for all s,t>0. The density is |u_t|^2+sum_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|^2 with Euclidean norms, and E(t) is its spatial Lebesgue integral, with no factor 1/2. No assertion at time zero is made.

definitions.type: spatial Laplace operator applied componentwise to u
definitions.definition: For x in R^n and t>0, Δ_xu(x,t)=sum_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t), component by component. The notation u_t,u_tt,∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}u_t denotes the corresponding classical partial derivatives on R^n×(0,∞). D_xu is the m-by-n matrix with columns ∂_{x_j}u, and |D_xu|^2 is its Frobenius square sum_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|^2. Vectors have the Euclidean dot product and norm. Spatial integrals are Lebesgue integrals on R^n; boxes carry the restricted Lebesgue measure. int denotes topological interior and 1_A denotes the indicator of a set A.
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+sum_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2, for x in R^n and t>0, with exactly the Euclidean and Frobenius normalization of problem.md:38-46.
For every t>0, E(t)=∫_{R^n} e(x,t) dx. This is the ordinary finite Lebesgue integral, used after spatial integrability has been established; there is no factor 1/2.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary x∈R^n and t>0. By H004 the identity u(x,r)·u(x,r)=1 holds for every r>0. H002 permits differentiating this scalar identity in r at t. The ordinary product rule for the finite Euclidean dot product gives 2u(x,t)·u_t(x,t)=0, hence u·u_t=0 at (x,t).

Choose a real scalar a at (x,t) from H005, so u_tt-Δ_xu=a u. Dot with u_t and use F001 and symmetry of the dot product: u_t·(u_tt-Δ_xu)=a(u_t·u)=0. This uses only a pointwise choice; no derivative or continuity of a is required.

Retain also the supplied explicit-equation calculation. Twice differentiating u·u=1 in time, using H002 and H004, gives 2|u_t|^2+2u·u_tt=0. Twice differentiating the same identity in each spatial coordinate gives 2|∂_{x_j}u|^2+2u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=0 for every j=1,...,n. Thus u·u_tt=-|u_t|^2 and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=-|∂_{x_j}u|^2. Dot the chosen normality equation with u. Since u·u=1, a=u·(u_tt-Δ_xu)=sum_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2. This computation applies to every scalar satisfying that equation at (x,t); substitute it back to obtain the explicit equation in the exported conclusion. Together with F001 and F002 these are all clauses of the exported conclusion. The point (x,t) was arbitrary, and the scalar witness's private identity does not occur in the resulting equation, so quantify over all x and t>0.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Then 0<t0/2<3t0/2<∞. Instantiate H006 with these endpoints and choose its compact C. Thus u(x,r)=q for every x outside C and every r∈J.

argument.text: A compact subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is bounded: the open boxes (-k,k)^n for positive integers k cover R^n and form an increasing family; compactness gives a finite subcover of C and therefore one containing box. For C empty any positive radius works. Consequently there exists R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n. This also exhibits the needed room between C and the boundary of the closed box.

produces.statement: There exists a real R>0 such that C⊂(-R,R)^n.

argument.text: Choose R>0 from F002 and set Q=[-R,R]^n. H001 ensures a finite positive number n of spatial coordinates. Q is compact and has Lebesgue measure (2R)^n<∞ by the rectangle formula. Since compact C is closed, (R^n\C)×int J is open. On that open set F001 says u is identically q. By H002 and locality of classical differentiation, every positive-order derivative of u is zero there: each component's difference quotients of a constant vanish, and this repeats for higher derivatives. Thus e,e_t and every derivative product listed in the exported conclusion vanish outside C at interior times.

produces.statement: Q=[-R,R]^n is compact with finite Lebesgue measure (2R)^n, C⊂int Q, and every positive-order derivative of u vanishes on (R^n\C)×int J.

argument.text: Smoothness H002 makes e,e_t, u_t·u_tt, and, for each j=1,...,n, u_t·∂_{x_j}u, ∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) continuous on R^n×(0,∞). At any fixed r∈int J, each is continuous and hence Borel measurable as a function of space. Its absolute value attains a finite bound on compact Q, and it is zero outside C by F003. Thus its absolute integral on R^n is at most its finite bound times |Q|=(2R)^n, proving integrability. These conclusions hold for every r∈int J and each spatial index. In particular t0∈int J, so e(·,t0) is integrable. Since t0 was arbitrary, e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0. The witnesses C,R and their definitions J,Q establish exactly the existential window assertion of the exported conclusion; none escapes as a globally fixed choice.

The scalar product rule and equality of mixed partial derivatives, valid because H002 is joint smoothness on the open space-time domain, give for every x∈R^n and r>0: e_t(x,r)=2u_t(x,r)·u_tt(x,r)+2sum_{j=1}^n∂_{x_j}u(x,r)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,r). argument.text: Choose such B from F003. Define the total function v(h,x)=(e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h when 0<|h|<eta, and v(h,x)=0 otherwise. The density is evaluated only at positive times in the first branch. Define bnd(x)=B 1_Q(x). Q is a measurable box of finite measure by F002; hence bnd is integrable and its absolute integral is B|Q|<∞.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary h∈R and x∈R^n. Temporarily assume L1: 0<|h|<eta. For x∈Q, apply M004 to the one-variable function r↦e(x,r) on the interval with endpoints min(t0,t0+h), max(t0,t0+h), and derivative r↦e_t(x,r). For purposes of the source's global domain R, extend both by zero at nonpositive times; the entire closed interval lies in (0,∞), where H002 and F001 give continuity and the asserted derivatives. The endpoints are distinct by L1. The source gives the difference quotient as e_t at an intervening time (the quotient is the same for either sign of h). By F003 its absolute value is at most B. For x∉Q, both densities vanish by F002, so the quotient is zero. The cases together prove |v(h,x)|≤B1_Q(x)=bnd(x). Discharge L1 and quantify over x and h to obtain: for all 0<|h|<eta and all x∈R^n, |v(h,x)|≤bnd(x).

produces.statement: For every real h with 0<|h|<eta and every x∈R^n, |v(h,x)|≤bnd(x).

argument.text: Let ell be the punctured-neighborhood filter at 0 in R. It is countably generated: the punctured intervals 0<|h|<1/k for positive integers k form a countable base. F004 gives strong measurability of v(h,·) for all sufficiently small nonzero h, and integrability of bnd. F005 gives domination everywhere in x for those h. For each x∈R^n, differentiability in time from H002 and F001 gives v(h,x)→e_t(x,t0) along ell. Instantiate M001 with X=R^n and Lebesgue measure, V=R, I=R, this ell, F(h)=v(h,·), f(x)=e_t(x,t0), and bound bnd. All these conditions hold pointwise or eventually as required, so ∫v(h,x)dx→∫e_t(x,t0)dx as h→0, h≠0.

For 0<|h|<eta, F002 ensures that both densities in v are integrable. By linearity of the Lebesgue integral and D003, ∫v(h,x)dx=(E(t0+h)-E(t0))/h. Thus F006 proves differentiability of the actual finite function E at t0, with E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0)dx. Substitute F001 and use the integrability of all its terms from F002 and linearity over the finite spatial sum: E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2sum_{j=1}^n∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. All integrands are evaluated at t0. The choices were available for arbitrary t0>0, so universal introduction proves every clause of the exported conclusion.

F004 proves strong measurability for 0<|h|<eta, which is an ell-eventual condition since eta>0.
F005 proves domination for every x for 0<|h|<eta; in particular it holds almost everywhere and ell-eventually.
F004 establishes integrability of bnd=B1_Q because Q is measurable of finite measure and B≥0 is finite.

For each fixed x, H002 and F001 identify the pointwise difference-quotient limit as e_t(x,t0); v is that quotient for ell-eventually all h. This pointwise conclusion implies the required almost everywhere convergence.

locals.declaration: Choose compact C from N002 at t0.
Together with C choose R>0 from N002 at t0.
Let Phi(y,s) be the point of R^n with j-th coordinate s and its other n-1 coordinates given by y in increasing coordinate order.
Fix an arbitrary vector y of the n-1 coordinates other than j.
For the fixed y, define phi(s)=g(Phi(y,s)).
Let Qother=[-R,R]^(n-1) in the remaining-coordinate space.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and a spatial index j∈{1,...,n}. H001 gives n≥1, so the remaining-coordinate space has dimension n-1≥0. Set J=[t0/2,3t0/2], choose C and R>0 from N002, and put Q=[-R,R]^n. Since t0∈int J, N002 gives integrability of the derivative products in the exported conclusion and of ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), all zero outside C. Also C⊂int Q and Q has finite measure.

produces.statement: At time t0 the functions ∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) are integrable on R^n and zero outside C; C⊂int Q, with C compact and Q=[-R,R]^n of finite measure.

argument.text: Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). By H002 it is smooth in x, and the product rule gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. It is zero off C by N002. As C is closed and contained in int Q, g is identically zero on the open complement of C, which contains the boundary of Q. Hence g vanishes on a neighborhood of that boundary. Define the coordinate insertion map Phi(y,s) by placing s in coordinate j and the vector y in the remaining coordinates, in increasing coordinate order.

produces.statement: g is smooth on R^n, zero on R^n\C, and ∂_{x_j}g(x)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)+u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) for every x∈R^n. In particular g is zero near the boundary of Q.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary y∈R^(n-1) and define phi(s)=g(Phi(y,s)) for s∈R. F002 and the chain rule give the derivative phi'(s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)) at every real s, including ±R. This derivative is continuous and hence bounded and Lebesgue interval-integrable on [-R,R]. Apply M003 with V=R, endpoints -R,R, f=phi, and derivative d(s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)). The integral equals phi(R)-phi(-R). Each endpoint has j-th coordinate ±R and is outside C⊂(-R,R)^n, so both values are zero by F002. Therefore ∫_{-R}^R ∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s))ds=0. Quantify over the arbitrary y. The oriented interval integral is the usual restricted Lebesgue integral here since -R<R, and including or deleting the singleton endpoints does not affect a Lebesgue integral.

Let Qother=[-R,R]^(n-1) and w(y,s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)). Splitting off coordinate j identifies Q with Qother×[-R,R]. Under Phi, Lebesgue measure on R^n is the product of Lebesgue measures on the remaining coordinates and on R: on every coordinate rectangle the image has exactly the product of the side lengths, and these rectangles generate the Borel sigma algebra; uniqueness of sigma-finite measures gives the identification, also for the completed Lebesgue integrals of the continuous functions used here. If n=1, the remaining-coordinate space is R^0, a singleton of measure 1, so the same statement holds. On the compact product box, w is continuous and bounded by F002, hence measurable and absolutely integrable. Its two summands from F002 have the same property, in agreement with F001. Apply M002 with X=R^(n-1), Y=R, V=R, the Lebesgue measures restricted to Qother and [-R,R], and f=w. These measures are finite, thus s-finite. The result and F003 yield ∫_Q∂_{x_j}g dx=∫_{Qother}(∫_{[-R,R]}w(y,s)ds)dy=∫_{Qother}0dy=0.

By F001 the derivative and both summands in F002 are zero outside Q, so their Q-integrals equal their R^n-integrals. Integrate the product rule F002, use F004 and linearity for the integrable summands from F001: 0=∫_{R^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{R^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx, all at time t0. Symmetry of the dot product and rearrangement prove ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx=-∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. The asserted integrability is part of F001. Since t0 and j were arbitrary this proves the exported conclusion.

applications.bindings: Set V=R, a=-R, b=R, f(s)=phi(s)=g(Phi(y,s)), d(s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)), at the current arbitrary remaining-coordinate vector y.
hypothesis_checks: R with its usual norm is a complete normed additive commutative group and real normed vector space.
F002 gives smooth g; the coordinate insertion map is affine with velocity the j-th coordinate vector, so the chain rule gives derivative d(s) at every s, in particular throughout [-R,R].
The same smoothness makes d continuous; on the compact interval [-R,R] it is bounded and measurable, giving finite absolute integral and interval integrability.

applications.bindings: Set X=R^(n-1) (remaining coordinates), Y=R (coordinate j), V=R, mu=Lebesgue measure restricted to Qother, nu=Lebesgue measure restricted to [-R,R], and f(y,s)=w(y,s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)).
hypothesis_checks: The spaces have their usual measurable structures, the two restricted Lebesgue measures are measures, and R has its standard real normed vector space structure. The coordinate/product measure identification is established in S004 using rectangle volumes and sigma-finite uniqueness.
Both restricted box measures are finite (including the dimension-zero singleton of measure 1 when n=1), hence s-finite.
F002 makes w continuous. It is bounded on compact Qother×[-R,R], and the product measure is finite, so its norm has finite integral; this proves product integrability before applying M002.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary t0>0. N002 supplies integrability of e(·,t0) and all derivative products below, and legitimizes the energy definition D003. N003 gives E'(t0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t·u_tt dx+2sum_{j=1}^n∫_{R^n}∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. Use N004 for each spatial index to obtain E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx-2sum_{j=1}^n∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. Linearity for this finite sum and D001 give E'(t0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t·(u_tt-Δ_xu)dx, with all integrands evaluated at t0. N001 says the last integrand is identically zero, hence E'(t0)=0.

produces.statement: E'(t0)=0, E is differentiable at t0, and e(·,t0) is integrable.

argument.text: The positive time t0 was arbitrary. By F001, for every r>0, e(·,r) is integrable and E is differentiable at r with E'(r)=0. This proves all requested analytic assertions, with no assertion at zero.

produces.statement: For every r>0, e(·,r) is integrable, E is differentiable at r, and E'(r)=0.

argument.text: For completeness retain the supplied final conservation statement. Fix s,t>0. If s=t, reflexivity gives E(t)=E(s). If s<t, F002 gives differentiability on (s,t) with derivative zero, and also continuity on [s,t], since E is differentiable at every positive time, including the endpoints. Apply M004 to E extended by zero at nonpositive arguments, derivative function identically zero, and endpoints s,t. It gives 0=(E(t)-E(s))/(t-s), hence E(t)=E(s), since t-s>0. If t<s, use the identical application with endpoints t,s and rearrange. All intervals lie strictly in (0,∞), so the extension never affects any value or derivative under consideration. Thus E is constant on (0,∞). Combining this with F002 proves the exported conclusion, with exactly the original density and normalization.

applications.bindings: For the branch s<t set f(r)=E(r) for r>0 and f(r)=0 otherwise, d(r)=0, a=s,b=t. For the branch t<s interchange the endpoints.
hypothesis_checks: The respective branch assumes strict endpoint order. The case s=t is handled by reflexivity without the source.

F002 gives differentiability of E at every positive point, hence continuity at all points of the closed interval between these positive endpoints; the extension agrees on an open neighborhood of that interval.
F002 gives E'(r)=0 at all interior points. Because the interval is positive, the extended function has exactly the same derivative there.
